soil-bio-226.title: Symbiosis, the long partnership of unlike organisms
soil-bio-226.text: In 1879 Heinrich Anton de Bary called it "the living together of unlike organisms." Symbiosis is any close, long-term interaction between two organisms of different species. Some writers keep the word for {{ref:soil-bio-251}}, where both partners benefit. A partnership can be obligate, meaning required, or facultative, meaning optional. An ectosymbiont lives on its partner, while an endosymbiont lives inside its tissues. {{ref:soil-bio-178}} in the roots of legumes are one example; nitrogen-fixing {{ref:soil-bio-200}} in alder roots is another. Not every link is friendly. Black walnut secretes juglone, which destroys many herbaceous plants within its root zone.

soil-bio-216.title: Hyphae, the threads that fungi grow by
soil-bio-216.text: The hyphae of the fungi in {{ref:soil-bio-166}} alone are estimated to stretch about 110 quadrillion kilometers through Earth's topsoils. A hypha is a long, branching filament of a fungus, an oomycete or an actinobacterium, like those in {{ref:soil-bio-012}}. It is one or more cells inside a tubular wall, usually of chitin. In most fungi, perforated cross-walls called septa divide it. Hyphae average 4–6 μm across and grow at their tips. In most {{ref:soil-bio-003}} they are the main mode of growth, and together they form a {{ref:soil-bio-217}}. Specialized forms include arbuscules, which trade nutrients with plant cells, and cords that move nutrients over long distances.

soil-bio-217.title: Mycelium, the hidden body of a fungus
soil-bio-217.text: A single Armillaria colony spans thousands of acres, while others are too small to see. Each is a mycelium, the root-like body of a fungus: a mass of branching, thread-like hyphae, described in {{ref:soil-bio-216}}. It feeds in two stages. Hyphae secrete enzymes that break polymers into small units such as monomers, then absorb them. Growing mycelia decompose plant material, add to the soil's organic fraction and release carbon dioxide. Their networks make up 20-30% of soil biomass, though traditional biomass measures fail to detect them. The mycelium of {{ref:soil-bio-157}} fungi helps most plants take up water and nutrients. By some estimates it receives well over 10% of the host's photosynthetic output. Many soil invertebrates eat mycelium. In compost, fungi break down the woody compound {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, which many other microbes cannot. They also degrade petroleum products and some farm chemicals, a cleanup described in {{ref:soil-env-033}}. Spread on logging roads, mycelium binds disturbed soil.

soil-bio-212.title: Termites, the engineers of tropical soils
soil-bio-212.text: The northern part of Kruger National Park alone holds about 1.1 million active termite nests rising as mounds. Termites are eusocial insects, living in cooperative colonies, that eat decaying plant material: mostly wood, leaf litter and soil humus. Primarily detritivores, they eat dead plants at any stage of decay. Higher termites also eat feces, humus, grass, leaves and roots. In subtropical and tropical regions they are important decomposers, and their recycling of wood and plant matter is of considerable ecological importance. Most species build underground colonies, using soil for their nests and mounds. Other nests are epigeal, built as mounds, or arboreal, in trees. Many species are ecosystem engineers. They change soil hydrology, decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth, and so the biodiversity around their large mounds. Of 3,014 classified species, 754 live in Africa, where mounds are fertile islands in savannas. Around 330 species of the Macrotermitinae farm Termitomyces fungi on their fecal pellets. Disturbance hits termites hard: loss of trees and soil cover, and trampling by cattle and goats, cut their diversity and abundance.

soil-bio-211.title: Millipedes, slow shredders of the forest floor
soil-bio-211.text: A single millipede species is estimated to eat between 1 and 11 percent of all leaf litter, depending on species and region. Millipedes are arthropods of the class Diplopoda, with two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments. Most are slow-moving detritivores of forest leaf litter that eat decaying leaves and dead wood. Some eat fungi or suck plant fluids. Their gut fragments litter and excretes it as pellets of leaf fragments, algae, fungi and bacteria, which helps microbes decompose it further. Their burrowing mixes organic with mineral matter. That makes them soil ecosystem engineers, especially where earthworms are scarce, as in some tropical forests.

soil-bio-229.title: How invading earthworms are eating North America's forest floor
soil-bio-229.text: Most northern forests of North America have had no native earthworms since the last ice age. The Wisconsin glaciation wiped them out, so a deep layer of dead leaves and litter became typical, and many native plants rely on it. From the 18th century, European worms arrived in soil with settlers, likely in the root balls of imported plants. Recreation, bait and construction now spread them, one case of {{ref:soil-bio-043}}. The invaders burrow, eat litter and leave casts, mixing nutrients beyond the reach of shallow roots, where they may be leached. The organic layer thins, nutrient release and decomposition speed up, and bulk density rises. Banded soils, {{ref:soil-class-138}}, lose their E horizons. Plant diversity, seedlings and mycorrhizal associations decline, while invasive plants such as buckthorn and garlic mustard increase. Asian jumping worms of Amynthas and Metaphire breed faster and live denser than European species, stripping the ground of organic matter. Worms cannot be removed from soil, so control aims to slow their spread: fewer bait releases, regulated soil movement and heat-treated compost or mulch.

soil-bio-207.title: Light or chemicals, rock or food: how life gets fed
soil-bio-207.text: Every living thing must answer three questions: where do its energy, its electrons and its carbon come from? The answers sort life into primary nutritional groups. Energy comes from light, for phototrophs, or from chemical compounds, for {{ref:soil-bio-205}}. Electrons come from organic donors, as in {{ref:soil-bio-206}}, or from inorganic ones, for lithotrophs. Carbon comes from organic compounds, for heterotrophs, or from carbon dioxide, for autotrophs. A name combines one term from each pair. A chemoorganoheterotroph, for example, takes its carbon from organic substrates and its energy from breaking down an organic compound. The pairs often travel together. Organisms that draw electrons from organic matter are often heterotrophs too, and lithotrophs are often autotrophs that use carbon dioxide. Plants count as lithotrophs because water is the electron donor of their photosynthesis. Cyanobacteria, algae and land plants are therefore photolithoautotrophs. Decomposers are chemoorganoheterotrophs, taking carbon and electrons from dead organic matter. All animals, fungi and protozoa, and some bacteria, are chemoheterotrophs. The labels are not always fixed: plants and some bacteria can switch between phototrophy and chemotrophy depending on the light. One distinction is easy to confuse. Aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration and fermentation describe the electron acceptor used, the substance that finally takes the electrons, and do not define a nutritional group.

soil-bio-205.title: Chemotrophs, life powered by chemistry instead of light
soil-bio-205.text: Hydrogen sulfide, ferrous iron and ammonia can all power life without sunlight. A chemotroph gets its energy by oxidizing electron donors from its surroundings, unlike phototrophs, which use light. The donors may be organic, for chemoorganotrophs, or inorganic, for chemolithotrophs. Chemoautotrophs build all their organic compounds from carbon dioxide; nitrifiers, methanogens and sulfur oxidizers are among them. Chemoheterotrophs, including most animals and fungi, cannot fix carbon themselves. Methanogens finish organic matter breakdown only once richer electron acceptors, oxygen, nitrate and sulfate, are used up. Thawing frozen soils is expected to raise their methane output.

soil-bio-219.title: Microbial ecology: studying microbes beyond medicine
soil-bio-219.text: {{ref:soil-hist-013}} studied microbes outside medicine. He discovered chemosynthesis, life powered by chemical energy. {{ref:soil-hist-016}} invented a way to grow chosen microbes, described in {{ref:soil-hist-017}}. {{ref:soil-hist-075}} recognized the bacteria behind three nitrogen processes: {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, {{ref:soil-fert-112}} and {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Their field is microbial ecology, also called environmental microbiology: the study of how microorganisms interact with their environment. Microbes drive the cycles of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and carbon, making nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium available in soil. Their relationships include {{ref:soil-bio-251}}, commensalism, amensalism and parasitism, all forms of living together first met in {{ref:soil-bio-226}}.

soil-bio-227.title: The microbiome, a community with an address
soil-bio-227.text: Up to 40% of the DNA sequenced from soil can be relic DNA, left behind by cells that are no longer alive. A microbiome is the community of microorganisms usually found living together in a given habitat. Whipps and colleagues first defined the term in 1988 while studying microorganisms of the {{ref:soil-bio-143}}. They described a characteristic community in a well-defined habitat with distinct physico-chemical properties. TerraGenome, a project to build a reference set of soil DNA, began in 2008. Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer may barely change which microbes make up a soil microbiome, yet it drastically reduces how connected their network is.

soil-bio-221.title: Metagenomics: reading the DNA of a whole soil at once
soil-bio-221.text: One gram of soil holds about 10^9–10^10 microbial cells, about one gigabase of genetic sequence. Metagenomics studies all the genetic material from all the organisms in such a sample, revealing their composition, diversity and functional potential. It needs no culturing. Early studies of environmental genes showed that growing microbes in the lab had missed most microbial diversity. Norman Pace proposed cloning DNA directly from environmental samples in 1985, and his group first reported doing so in 1991. Sequencing only marker genes such as 16S rRNA, the method of {{ref:soil-bio-262}}, shows which taxa are present. Metagenomics sequences all the DNA, so it also recovers enzymes and pathways. Soil communities are among the most complex known. Because sampling is uncontrolled, the most abundant organisms dominate shotgun sequence data. Functional metagenomics explores plant–microbe interactions and what uncultivated or rare members do in nutrient cycling and plant growth. Long-read sequencing of soils in industrial zones showed that chronic heavy metal contamination restructures the soil microbial community.

soil-bio-218.title: Geomicrobiology: microbes that make and break minerals
soil-bio-218.text: Some bacteria gain energy by reducing dissolved metal ions, and as a side effect they concentrate those metals into what can become ore deposits. This is the territory of geomicrobiology, the field between geology and microbiology. It studies the role of microbes in geological and geochemical processes, and the effects of minerals and metals on microbes. Its interactions run through rocks, minerals, soils, sediments, the atmosphere and the hydrosphere. There microbes drive the cycling of elements, precipitate and dissolve minerals and concentrate metals. In soil they change the speciation, or chemical form, of minerals and metals, along with their toxicity and mobility. They immobilize and detoxify metals, radionuclides, sulfur and phosphorus. Chromium shows the payoff. Cr(VI) is mobile and toxic, while Cr(III) is less toxic and precipitates in soils above pH 6. Microbial reduction of Cr(VI) is therefore a low-cost way to clean up soil, a form of {{ref:soil-env-023}}. Sulfate-reducing bacteria precipitate metals as sulfides and add bicarbonate alkalinity that neutralizes acid mine drainage. Applications include pollution cleanup, mining, slowing climate change and drinking water supply.

soil-bio-225.title: Streptomyces, the bacteria that make soil smell like soil
soil-bio-225.text: The earthy odor of soil comes from geosmin, a volatile compound released by Streptomyces. This is the largest genus of actinomycete bacteria, found mainly in soil and decaying vegetation. They are filamentous, Gram-positive bacteria with branched hyphae 0.5–2.0 μm across. Their substrate mycelium scavenges organic compounds, and most produce spores. Streptomycetes make over two-thirds of the clinically useful natural antibiotics; streptomycin is named after the genus. Several species are plant pathogens, causing scab of potatoes and soft rot of sweet potatoes.

soil-bio-224.title: Azotobacter, the nitrogen fixer that works alone
soil-bio-224.text: Azotobacter survives in dry soil as cysts for up to 24 years. This genus of aerobic, free-living soil bacteria fixes atmospheric nitrogen and release it into the soil as ammonium. Unlike {{ref:soil-bio-239}}, it needs no plant partner, and fixation stops when ammonium or nitrate is available. It favors neutral and weakly basic soils, not acid ones. It shields its oxygen-sensitive nitrogen-fixing enzyme, {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, by speeding up its metabolism. Besides the molybdenum-iron enzyme, it has a vanadium one that works down to 5 °C. {{ref:soil-hist-016}} described the genus in 1901. It makes auxins, a kind of {{ref:soil-bio-245}}, and goes into azotobacterin, a {{ref:soil-fert-048}}.

soil-bio-203.title: Bacterivores, the grazers of the microbial world
soil-bio-203.text: Some bacteria are never eaten: the spores of Clostridium perfringens are one example. A bacterivore gets its energy and nutrients mainly or entirely by eating bacteria. The term mostly covers free-living microscopic heterotrophs such as nematodes, amoebae and other protozoa. Some larger invertebrates, certain arthropods among them, eat bacteria too, and springtails are listed among bacterivores. Many are generalist predators of any bacteria, though not all bacteria are easily digested. In the lab, bacterivores contaminating samples hinder the growing of bacteria for study. Cycloheximide can suppress them but also inhibits some anaerobic prokaryotes.

soil-bio-204.title: Fungivory: the many creatures that eat fungi
soil-bio-204.text: Beetles, ants and termites each took up fungus farming 40 to 60 million years ago. Today about 330 termite species cultivate Termitomyces fungi in their nests. Fungivory, or mycophagy, is the eating of fungi, and organisms that eat nothing else are fungivores. Fungus eaters include birds, mammals, insects, plants, amoebae, snails, slugs, nematodes, bacteria and other fungi. Trichoderma fungi detect other fungi, bind to their hyphae and digest their cell walls with enzymes such as chitinases. They have protected crops from pathogens such as Rhizoctonia solani. Bacterial mycophagy, a term coined in 2005, means bacteria growing at the expense of living fungal hyphae.

soil-bio-214.title: Fossorial animals, the diggers that remake soil
soil-bio-214.text: Ants, termites and earthworms move so much soil that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift. Such burrowers are fossorial animals: adapted to digging and living mainly, though not only, underground. Moles, badgers, naked mole-rats, armadillos and wombats are examples, as are many clams, beetles, wasps, bees and spiders. Their digging, a form of {{ref:soil-bio-047}}, changes soil composition, structure and vegetation, usually shifting plant species and raising plant diversity. Mounds and bare burrowed soils hold more ammonium and nitrate than vegetated soils. They also have a greater potential to turn ammonium into nitrate, mainly because the grass cover is gone.

soil-bio-213.title: Termite mounds, earthen towers built by insects
soil-bio-213.text: The largest termite mound on record measured 12.8 meters. Termite mounds are nests that protrude above the soil surface, built of earth and mud and stronger than underground nests. Macrotermes builds some of the largest, 8 to 9 meters high, with chimneys, pinnacles and ridges. Compass termites build wedge-shaped mounds aligned north–south, which warm quickly in the morning but avoid overheating at midday. Mounds are rich in clay, so where rain is torrential and continuous they risk erosion. They shelter birds, lizards, snakes and scorpions, and 54 ant species are known to live in Nasutitermes mounds.

soil-bio-228.title: The detrital food web, where most food ends up
soil-bio-228.text: Most of what an ecosystem's plants produce is never eaten. Instead it is recycled through {{ref:soil-bio-112}}, the dead remains of living things, into useful nutrients. That means any non-living organic matter: leaf litter, dead wood, carrion, dead microbes and feces among others. In a detrital food web, decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break it down, and it passes to detritivores and then to carnivores. Raymond Lindeman emphasized the soil's decomposer community among the basal species of food webs. This web links to the grazing web. Mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat earthworms that consume decaying leaves.

soil-bio-206.title: Organotrophs, which take their electrons from food
soil-bio-206.text: Animals and many bacteria share a habit: they pull their electrons from organic matter. An organotroph obtains hydrogen or electrons from organic substrates. Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946 to classify microorganisms by how they obtain electrons for respiration. Many organotrophs, animals and many bacteria among them, are also heterotrophs, and they can be aerobic or anaerobic. The counterpart is the lithotroph, which takes its electrons from inorganic substrates. Both terms belong to the scheme of {{ref:soil-bio-207}}.
